results.title: A Primer on Uncertainty and Calibration in Deep Learning
results.content: For example, instead of saying: *“The house price is 480,000,”a well-calibrated model would say: “The price is 480,000 ± 70,000 , but I’m really not confident because the location is novel to me.” And that ± 70,000 is where uncertainty kicks in.* Hence, uncertainty in deep learning is the **lack of confidence a model has in its predictions**, typically arising from **incomplete information, ambiguous data, or limitations in the model itself** (this shouldn’t be confused with confidence value model gives as output, though ideally it should, this discrepancy in expected and actual behaviour of model logits/probability/scores is comes under model calibration, this also will be covered in latter sections). A deterministic model makes a point prediction `y=f(x`), but a probabilistic or uncertainty-aware model outputs a **distribution** over possible predictions: `y∼p(y∣x).` Uncertainty is then quantified via: * **Variance**, entropy, or confidence intervals in regression * **Predictive entropy** or margin in classification That said, lets start diving into core concepts. ### Method 1 : Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) This simplest way of modelling this type of uncertainty is by predicting not just a mean output `μ(x)` but also a corresponding variance `σ2(x)`, treating the output as a Gaussian distribution: \(y^∼N(μ(x),σ2(x))\) During training, we use *Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)*, leading to the following Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss: \(\mathcal{L}\_{\text{NLL}} = \frac{1}{2\sigma²(x)} (y -\mu(x))² + \frac{1}{2} \log \sigma²(x)\) This formulation naturally balances error (left term) and uncertainty (right term containing `σ)`. Conversely, a model may express confident predictions (low uncertainty) but be overconfident and hence **badly mis-calibrated**. #### Ensembles and Dropout Both methods, discussed earlier for epistemic uncertainty, naturally improve calibration: * **Ensembles** smooth out extreme predictions across models * **Dropout at test time** simulates stochastic ensembles These methods reduce **variance** and act as regularizers, especially useful when used with temperature scaling. #### Prediction Interval Plots For regression models, especially those predicting both mean and variance (e.g., heteroscedastic regression), we can plot: * Confidence intervals (e.g., 90%, 95%) This reveals how uncertainty expands or contracts with input domain shifts, and whether **the intervals actually cover the target**, which speaks to coverage and calibration.

results.title: Calibration (statistics) - HandWiki
results.content: # Calibration (statistics). * procedures in statistical classification to determine class membership probabilities which assess the uncertainty of a given new observation belonging to each of the already established classes. For example, model calibration can be also used to refer to Bayesian inference about the value of a model's parameters, given some data set, or more generally to any type of fitting of a statistical model. Calibration in classification means turning transform classifier scores into class membership probabilities. An overview of calibration methods for two-class and multi-class classification tasks is given by Gebel (2009). A classifier might separate the classes well, but be poorly calibrated, meaning that the estimated class probabilities are far from the true class probabilities. In this case, a calibration step may help improve the estimated probabilities. A variety of metrics exist that are aimed to measure the extent to which a classifier produces well-calibrated probabilities. Recent variants include the Adaptive Calibration Error (ACE) and the Test-based Calibration Error (TCE) which address limitations of the ECE metric that may arise when classifier scores concentrate on narrow subset of the [0,1] range. The following univariate calibration methods exist for transforming classifier scores into class membership probabilities in the two-class case:. The *calibration problem* in regression is the use of known data on the observed relationship between a dependent variable and an independent variable to make estimates of other values of the independent variable from new observations of the dependent variable. The following multivariate calibration methods exist for transforming classifier scores into class membership probabilities in the case with classes count greater than two:. * Calibrated probability assessment – Subjective probabilities assigned in a way that historically represents their uncertainty. *Multivariate calibration of classifier scores into the probability space* (PDF) (PhD thesis). Hauskrecht, Obtaining well calibrated probabilities using bayesian binning. "Towards a Rigorous Calibration Assessment Framework: Advancements in Metrics, Methods, and Use." ECAI 2023. Obtaining Well Calibrated Probabilities Using Bayesian Binning. (1994) *Measurement, Regression and Calibration*, OUP. H. (2008) "Calibration Intervals in Linear Regression Models", *Communications in Statistics - Theory and Methods*, 37 (11), 1688–1696. J. (2003) "The regression-calibration method for fitting generalized linear models with additive measurement error", *Stata Journal*, 3 (4), 361–372.

results.title: Evaluating the Quality of the Quantified Uncertainty for (Re)Calibration of Data-Driven Regression Models
results.content: Any other value provides little insight into how well-calibrated the model truly is, making it difficult to set specific target values as optimization goals – unlike accuracy metrics such as the mean absolute error, where a given threshold can be meaningfully interpreted with respect to the target value domain. The model is trained to minimize the Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss (see Section 3.5Calibration of Data-Driven Regression Models")), which allows each ensemble to output both a mean prediction and an associated predictive variance, assuming Gaussian-distributed uncertainty. The remaining metrics – Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP), Coverage Width Criterion (CWC), Expected Normalized Calibration Error (ENCE), and Uncertainty Calibration Error (UCE) – exhibit less consistent behavior. As in the recalibration case study (Section 4.3Calibration of Data-Driven Regression Models")), we focus on changes in metric values exceeding a relative threshold of 3%. Our results suggest that calibration metrics can reliably detect miscalibration effects when evaluated on datasets with at least 500–1000 samples, assuming typical number of bins for binning-based approaches (e.g., 10 bins).

results.title: Evaluating and Calibrating Uncertainty Prediction in ...
results.content: We chose as a test case for our calibration method, the direct approach for producing uncertainty: we transform the network output from a single scalar to a Gaussian distribution by taking the scalar as the mean and adding a branch that predicts the standard deviation (STD) as in [16]. Based on this deﬁnition, we propose a new calibration evaluation metric similar to the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) [18], which groups examples into interval bins with similar uncertainty, and then measures the discrepancy between each bin’s parameters and the parameters of the empirical distribution within the bin. Finally, we propose a calibration method where we re-adjust the predicted uncertainty, in our case the outputted Gaussian variance, by minimizing the negative-log-likelihood (NLL) on a separate re-calibration set. Figure 4 shows the resulting reliability diagrams before calibration (predicted uncertainty) and after (calibrated uncertainty) for all four positional outputs, on the validation set consisting of 37K object instances.

results.title: Uncertainty Quantification Metrics for Deep Regression
results.content: When deploying deep neural networks on robots or other physical systems, the learned model should reliably quantify predictive uncertainty. Using synthetic regression datasets, we look into how those metrics behave under four typical types of uncertainty, their stability regarding the size of the test set, and reveal their strengths and weaknesses. As such, the NLL can also be used as a metric for uncertainty predictions, since a model with a lower NLL does a better job (in expectation) of fitting the true data distribution. For estimating predictive uncertainty, Deep Ensemble (DE) [4] is a simple yet effective method that trains multiple models in the same architecture with different random initialization and data shuffling. In practice, for the regression task, each individual model outputs two scalars, which are interpreted as the mean and variance of a Gaussian distribution, and then it is trained to minimize the Gaussian NLL loss as in (12 ‣ III-C Regression Models with Uncertainty Predictions ‣ III Theory ‣ Uncertainty Quantification Metrics for Deep Regression")) on the training set. For each dataset with different types of uncertainty, we compute all metrics for both our models on the test sets. Homoscedastic and Heteroscedastic datasets: we first look at the predicted density distribution in Fig. 3 (a) and (b) for each model. Interestingly, AUSE seems to imply that the EBR model has learned a distribution that is better than the ground truth of the homoscedastic dataset. This highlights the main difference between AUSE (and Spearman correlation) and calibration error/NLL: AUSE measures a correlation between uncertainty and the absolute error, while calibration error and NLL measure how well the learned distribution captures the data. Limitations: The value is not bounded thus, lacks interpretability; It may fail in tasks where homoscedastic uncertainty is dominant, which is rare in real-world applications; It does not comply with distribution prediction approach since the generating distribution does not return optimal AUSE. Essentially calibration error and NLL measure how well the predicted probability distribution corresponds to the true data generating distribution, whereas AUSE and Spearman measure how well the predicted uncertainty can tell the magnitude of errors.
